data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001's 'negative evidence' criterion for distinguishing genuine reliability from mere checklist compliance is both under- and over-inclusive relative to the problem's requirement. It is over-inclusive because a panel could correctly mark items N/A or Modified for bad reasons (e.g., misunderstanding an item), yielding 'negative evidence' that tracks the right answer without genuine discriminatory skill. It is under-inclusive because a well-designed checklist for tasks with objectively verifiable outcomes may require every item on a given case, so no N/A/Modified markings exist—yet the panel's correct answer could still represent genuine reliability (e.g., robust independent agreement) rather than 'lucky compliance.' By conditioning genuine reliability on the presence of N/A/Modified deviations, SRC_001 cannot classify a full-compliance correct judgment as genuine even when it is, and risks classifying lucky deviations as genuine. This fails the problem's ask for evidence that distinguishes genuine gain from compliance that merely happens to track the right answer.
